chapter: Decca, Cow Cow Blues and royalties
title: Playing with Sister Rosetta Tharpe for Decca
summary: Price recounts how Milt Gabler and Mayo Williams brought him to Rosetta Tharpe, the hit 'Two Little Fishes' and his terms for working with her.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: When you got with Decca, you did a lot of stuff also... you did things with gospel singers.
Sister Rosetta Tharpe and so on...

I'll tell you how that came about, Dan. You know, early I told you that I came from a long line of religious singers and you could be banished from the clan if you sang gospel songs or if you sang songs in a rhythm and that thing, you know what I mean. Although, back in those days, the Church of God in Christ people were doing it, but they were doing it in a church atmosphere. Church background and church setting. So finally, one day Milt Gabler asked Mayo to have me come down to see him. And a guy had written a song called, "Two Little Fishes and Five Loaves of Bread." It wasn't really a gospel song but it was about, you know, about the Lord taking the fishes and

whatever he did with them and all. So they asked me would I consider to work with Rosetta Tharpe. Well you know Rosetta Tharpe tuned her guitar funny and sang in the wrong key and the meter sometimes were not exact. She could sing and all that, but then she was a folk singer more or less. So I told Mayo I'd have to think about it. And then he sent...they sent Rosetta Tharpe's mother to see me and to explain to me that if a song were played, if the mind teaching was right, then that was not against that feeling that I had, you know what I mean, that there's nothing wrong with that as long as my intention was right... 'cause I knew I wasn't going to play anything but the blues anyway. You know, and Boogie-Woogie, and mix it up and play jazz. So then I was reluctant, and so finally they said, "okay, let's try." So we made "Two Little Fishes and Five Loaves of Bread" and it was a big hit. "Up Above My Head" on the opposite side. And we did. Now, they don't want me. They only want to give me $100 a record. Then Rosetta would take the song and go out on the road for personal appearances and say that she got The Sam Price trio with her, and it would not be so. So I just decided to make a business out of it. I just said, "Okay, you come to town, if you make ten songs you owe me a thousand dollars; I'll work three days a week with you, straighten it out and, you know what I mean, straighten it out, and

I'll get the musicians. I'll take care of everything, you don't have to worry. Oh, I'd show her how to move that fret up on her guitar so it'd be in the right key, show her how to...just let her play her heart out, and I would play with her, you know, and make the musicians play, and I use good jazz musicians. And I think that that was one of the things --- (recording interruption) Now where were we?
With Rosetta Tharpe and you said you made that arrangement with her that...

Well I made it with Decca because she didn't want to pay me. And never...Rosetta Tharpe never gave me a Christmas card. And I made her a lot of money. You see, Dan, this is the thing about my piano playing-- if my piano can benefit somebody, I'm not jealous.
